cards.title: Use a Job Statement as an Alignment Compass
cards.summary: A clearly articulated job statement acts as a two-sided compass: it aligns both the customer's problem and the internal job spec, enabling autonomous employee decisions.
cards.use_when: When an ecommerce team's roadmap or feature debates lack a shared anchor, or when employees need to make day-to-day tradeoffs without escalation.
steps: Write the job your customers are hiring you to solve as a short statement in verbs and nouns (not adjectives).
Treat the statement as a two-sided compass: one side points to deeper understanding of the customer's job, the other to the job spec (features, processes) that must align with it.
When an unplanned issue or opportunity surfaces, test it against the compass heading: if it clearly intersects the job, let people act without asking permission.
Expect energized, self-directed action rather than 'don't give me one more thing' resistance — the source reports this pattern at OnStar, Intuit and SNHU.
Revisit the statement periodically so the job spec side keeps up with the evolving customer side.
caveats: The source presents this as observed pattern across several organizations, not a guaranteed outcome.
A vague job statement in adjectives ('be convenient') fails as a compass.
People whose work doesn't align with the job may need to be restructured or counseled out, per the Deseret News example.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Jobs Focus Produces Four Organizational Benefits
cards.summary: An organization explicitly focused on a well-defined job enjoys distributed decision making, resource optimization, inspiration, and better measurement.
cards.use_when: When making the business case for job-based positioning, or when restructuring teams, budgets or KPIs around customer jobs.
steps: Distributed decision making: empower employees throughout the organization to make decisions that align with the job, so they can be autonomous and innovative without waiting for top-down direction.
Resource optimization: audit where resources are currently allocated against what matters most to the job; rebalance toward job-critical work and away from misaligned activities.

Inspiration: connect work to how it lets real people make progress in their lives — the source reports engineers working hard because they knew lives were at stake, not because they were told to work nights and weekends.
Better measurement: let a job focus pull the team toward more customer-centric metrics rather than only easy-to-capture internal numbers.
Articulate the job in mission and communications, and drive it deeply into culture over time — the source says this is difficult, takes real work, but pays off.
caveats: The source describes these as benefits observed across successful organizations, not a guaranteed sequence.
Embedding jobs in culture is described as slow and effortful; expect resistance from parts of the organization.
Operational efficiency still matters — the source argues it is only value-creating when it serves a high-priority job.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Culture Built on the Job Enables Unprompted Action
cards.summary: When employees deeply understand the job, they clear roadblocks on their own; the leader's role is to build structures that let those choices happen.
cards.use_when: When designing customer-service or support empowerment policies, or when deciding how much discretion front-line staff should have.
steps: Make the job explicit enough that staff can judge whether an action serves it.
Give front-line employees authority to act on that judgment without approval — SNHU advisers independently arranged grocery gift cards and a hospital diploma presentation for students in need.
Treat those unprompted actions as consistent with the job, not as policy violations.
As leader, focus on creating structures and culture that make the right choices natural, rather than scripting every case.
Use job clarity as the mechanism for waste reduction: once everyone is aligned, wasted time, energy and resources are minimized systematically (the 'lean' effect LeBlanc describes).
caveats: Examples are drawn from higher education (SNHU), not ecommerce; the transferable mechanism is discretion bounded by job clarity.
Unbounded discretion is not the claim — actions were still consistent with an explicit job.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Replace Generic Mission Statements with Job Statements
cards.summary: A well-crafted statement of the jobs a company exists to solve can be both inspiring and practical, unlike generic mission statements.
cards.use_when: When rewriting a company mission, vision or internal rallying cry so it actually guides decisions.
steps: Identify the most important job or jobs your organization exists to solve for customers.
Express the statement in verbs and nouns describing customer progress, not abstract aspirations like 'be more honest' or 'deliver convenience'.
Use the jobs statement rather than a generic mission statement as the rallying cry that aligns individuals across functions.
Check breadth of understanding: ask whether the jobs are understood across the organization and reflected in leadership and corporate communications.
Reinforce it as an enduring innovation North Star in leadership communications and culture.
Use shorthand phrases to keep the standard honest — American Girl used 'story, not stuff'; Deseret News used 'we are not the Sacramento Bee'.
caveats: The source warns against generic mission statements but still says articulation requires real work and deep cultural embedding.
Shorthand rallying cries only work when the underlying job is genuinely understood.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Measure What Improves Customers' Lives, Not Just What's Easy
cards.summary: Companies tend to measure easily captured data and miss whether they are improving customers' lives; measure the job-relevant outcome instead.
cards.use_when: When choosing KPIs or analytics dashboards for an ecommerce business, or when data is abundant but feels disconnected from customer value.
steps: Audit current metrics: identify which ones exist mainly because they roll off servers easily (traffic, screens, frequency, conversion rates).
Identify what outcome the customer is actually hiring you for — Intuit's accountants hire software to save time on tax returns so they can take more clients or gain free time.
Ask directly whether the product is helping customers achieve that outcome, even when the outcome is hard to measure.
Add job-relevant measures alongside efficiency measures rather than replacing them — measure what matters while still improving efficiency.

Pressure-test with a single customer-centric question if needed: SNHU keeps 'would graduates do it all over again?' front and center (95% said yes as of early 2016) while still tracking reams of micro-level data.
Watch for internal filters (business units, segments) that build data models which rarely map to customer jobs.
caveats: The source argues data reflects the biases of whoever chose what to collect and discard; treat internal metrics as models, not reality.
Hard-to-measure outcomes still matter profoundly; the 95% figure is an example from SNHU, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Amazon-Style Job Metrics with Automatic Price Adjustment
cards.summary: Amazon anchors its retail business on three customer job measures — vast selection, low prices, fast delivery — monitored minute by minute and treated as defect-free requirements.
cards.use_when: When designing monitoring and enforcement systems for a core customer promise such as price competitiveness or delivery speed.
steps: Define the small set of promises that matter in your retail business, as Amazon did with selection, price and delivery speed.
Build automation that enforces the promise continuously — Amazon's shopping robot scours prices of hundreds of benchmark products twice daily and automatically lowers its price to beat competitors.
Expect visible consequences: a lower price can appear while an item sits in a customer's cart.
Set a gross-margin threshold below which the automatic price change triggers human review rather than proceeding silently.
Treat delays or misses in the promise as defects to be eradicated, not accidents or ordinary underperformance.
Keep the system efficiency-focused but aimed squarely at the job customers hire you to do.
caveats: This describes Amazon's system as reported by the authors; your margins, product set and competitor set differ — don't copy the threshold.
Requires reliable benchmark price data and automation; manual equivalents may not keep pace.
Check your local pricing and competition regulations before implementing automatic undercutting.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Separate the Distinct Jobs a Product Is Hired For
cards.summary: Traditional products often bundle several different customer jobs and do none well, hiding what people actually hire them to do.
cards.use_when: When an established product or channel is losing ground and you need to decide which jobs to double down on and which to abandon.
steps: List the distinct jobs your product or channel has historically been hired for (for newspapers: breaking news, classified employment and low-cost item ads, opinion alignment).
Ask whether each job is now better served by other solutions — the Boston Marathon bombing showed print was beaten on breaking news by TV, live blogs and Twitter.
Without the jobs lens, teams muddle all jobs together and can't tell which solution remains distinctive.
Choose the job(s) where you can still be distinctive and stop spending resources on jobs for which you are no longer relevant.
Use the job definition to filter coverage and scope: Deseret News covered 5 family-relevant legislative issues rather than all thirty bills on the A1 page.
Expect a realignment cost: some staff won't accept the focus and may need restructuring or counseling out.
caveats: This is a strategic triage process, not a quick optimization; the Deseret News example took years and organizational change.
Abandoning a job can mean losing customers and staff who valued the old bundle.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use Functional, Emotional and Social Lenses on the Job
cards.summary: Define a job through its functional, emotional and social dimensions, since customers often hire a solution for the emotional payoff on top of a functional task.
cards.use_when: When writing positioning or creative strategy and the functional benefit alone doesn't explain customer attachment.
steps: State the functional job plainly: Deseret News readers needed deeper analysis after an event was already reported — 'Perspective, Insight, Context and Analysis' (PICA).
Layer the emotional dimension: readers wanted to be well-informed, confident in their knowledge, and true to their beliefs so they could make a difference at home and in their community.
Identify the social dimension: connecting with like-minded readers and community members.
Check whether your current solution serves only the functional layer while competitors or adjacent products supply the emotional payoff.

Build content, community and distribution around the emotional benefit rather than around the product format — Deseret built Facebook communities around faith and family themes, saying social strategy around the job opened a much broader audience than the newspaper product ever could have.
caveats: The Deseret News social growth figures (low millions to over 100 million followers through its FamilyShare Network) come from one organization's reported results and should be treated as an example, not a benchmark.
Emotional framing that doesn't match a real job is positioning decoration, not Jobs Theory.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Segment by Job, Not Demographics
cards.summary: A segment can be large, distinct and underserved yet invisible to demographic and psychographic segmentation because it is defined by a shared job.
cards.use_when: When demographic or psychographic segments aren't producing differentiated messaging, or when a promising audience seems 'unfindable' by standard targeting.
steps: Start with a suspected demographic segment and then test whether a job explains behavior better — Deseret's process began as demographic segmentation and became jobs-based segmentation.
Define the job in customer terms: 'I want to be well-informed, feel more confident in my knowledge, and still be true to my beliefs so I can make a difference in my home and community.'
Map subgroups that share the job even when their surface attributes differ — Deseret grouped tolerant believers, devoted denominationalists and strugglers as 'like-minded believers'.
Check size and saturation: the source reports this group was nearly 56% of American news consumers and felt massively underserved.
Verify the job's emotional tension — Deseret readers consumed both the New York Times and Sean Hannity and hated both, wanting rigor without disconnect from their values and values without polemic.
Build message and offering to the job rather than the demographic profile.
caveats: The 56% figure is one research finding about American news consumers, not a general benchmark.
Job-based segments may be invisible to standard ad targeting; you may need to reach them through behavior or interest signals instead.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Watch for Organizational Drift Away from the Job
cards.summary: As companies grow, the organizing unit shifts from the customer's job to internal processes, products, competitors and investors, creating an edited view of the customer.
cards.use_when: When a scaling ecommerce business's processes, org chart or reporting feel increasingly detached from what customers want.
steps: Recognize the baseline: successful start-ups are organized around the customer's job — small teams wearing multiple hats who share an understanding of what enables customer progress.

Recognize the drift: growth requires layers of management and defined processes, and the organizing unit moves to focus on customers-as-data, products, competitors and investors, with less focus on the job.
Notice the specific risk: managers frame their task as efficiently executing internal processes rather than effectively resolving customers' jobs.
Counter it by keeping managers close to the customer context; distance makes it easier to adopt a highly edited view of the external world.
Audit 'competencies' that were once job-serving but are now just internally benchmarked capabilities being optimized for their own sake.
Keep operational efficiency, but require it to create customer value by fulfilling a high-priority job.

Use one simple unifying question in disputes: 'What are our customers hiring us to do?' — the source reports that internal disagreement about spreadsheets or campaigns is fine, but nobody should be debating the job.
caveats: Efficiency and process discipline are not the enemy — the source says functional oversight is a requirement of competitive markets.
This is a persistent structural drift, not a one-time fix; expect to re-audit as you grow.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Validate a Job Statement by Abstraction Level
cards.summary: A valid job statement is expressed in verbs and nouns and can be solved by candidates from multiple, different product categories.
cards.use_when: When checking whether a job statement is genuinely a job, or when a team's 'job' is really a preference, a spec or an aspiration.
steps: Reject job statements made of adjectives and adverbs. 'Convenience' is not a job — it may be an experience that causes a customer to choose you, but it isn't the job.
Express the job in verbs and nouns, e.g. 'I need to write books verbally, obviating the need to type or edit by hand.'
Apply the category test: if the architecture of the product or system can only be met by products within the same product class, you haven't found a job.

Move up one level of abstraction until candidates come from different categories. 'A 12-ounce chocolate milkshake in a disposable container' is not a job; 'keep me occupied with what's happening on the road while I drive and fill me up so I'm not hungry during a 10am meeting' is, because a banana, doughnuts, bagels, a Snickers or coffee could all be hired.

Distinguish technical specifications from jobs: a spec such as a thin sheet with a high coefficient of friction and low thermal conduction is not a job; the underlying job is keeping the family warm and dry through Boston winters and summers while minimizing heating and cooling costs — which wood pulp, fiberglass, Tyvek, dehumidifiers and fans or even relocating could all serve.
Do this work seriously — the source insists calling something a job should not roll off the tongue with minimal thought.
caveats: Setting the right level of abstraction is described as more art than science; expect iteration.
Jobs theory is bounded — applying 'job' to every human motivation dilutes its clarity and predictability.
The theory was built inductively and its author explicitly says anomalies are useful signals of its boundaries, not disproof.
